learning_outcomes.text: By the end of the course, students will know: manufacturing systems and production processes, understanding the advantages and limitations of process and plant design choices in different application contexts.
By the end of the course, students will know: current topics concerning the organization and management of the technical factors of production.

By the end of the course, students will know: the broader multidisciplinary context of engineering, with particular emphasis on problem solving, starting from the problem to identify its causes and possible countermeasures.

By the end of the course, students will know: the techniques and methods applicable to the design of industrial plants and service facilities together with their limitations, including awareness of the non-technical implications of engineering practice.

By the end of the course, students will be able to: select and use appropriate equipment, tools and methods for the design and production of goods and services, including calculation tools for the sizing of service facilities and logistics systems.

By the end of the course, students will be able to: combine theory and practice to solve multidisciplinary engineering problems, taking into account both technical and non-technical constraints and collaborating with the professionals typically involved in manufacturing companies.

By the end of the course, students will be able to: analyse data and information (demand series, plant performance) using established methods and tools, interpreting results and drawing consistent conclusions.

By the end of the course, students will be able to: compare alternative solutions to plant engineering problems — location, layout and sizing alternatives — contributing to technically justified decisions in compliance with industry standards and procedures.
By the end of the course, students will be able to: work collaboratively and effectively within a team, recognizing the interdisciplinary implications of the problem addressed.
By the end of the course, students will be able to: organize their work while meeting assigned deadlines, managing available time and resources.
By the end of the course, students will be able to: recognize personal knowledge limitations, identifying appropriate information sources and guided learning opportunities.
Students will be able to: communicate information, problems and solutions in the field of industrial plants to both specialist and non-specialist audiences, using appropriate technical language.
Students will be able to: present problems, analyses and results clearly and systematically through written reports in standard formats.
Students will be able to: graphically represent and communicate technical data, results and solutions through diagrams, graphs and tables.
Students will be able to: acquire and update their knowledge in the field of industrial plants, also independently, using established educational resources.
Students will be able to: identify and consult bibliographic sources and technical documentation, selecting relevant information.
Students will be able to: learn through problem solving applied to real cases of appropriate complexity.

Students will be able to: understand and interpret the fundamental principles of design, production and maintenance processes, in compliance with quality, safety and reliability requirements and with reference to the main technical and environmental standards.

By the end of the course, students will know: current topics in the organization and management of production factors, together with quantitative methodologies for profitability analysis and for the optimisation of production factors.

By the end of the course, students will know: the broader multidisciplinary context of engineering, with a focus on problem solving, starting from the problem to identify its causes and possible countermeasures.

By the end of the course, students will know: the techniques and methods applicable to plant and industrial logistics design — demand forecasting, layout study, warehouse sizing — together with their limitations.
By the end of the course, students will know: the non-technical implications of engineering practice, including the economic and safety implications of plant design choices.

By the end of the course, students will be able to: select and use appropriate equipment, tools and methods for the production of goods and services, such as material handling, storage and identification systems.

By the end of the course, students will be able to: combine theory and practice to solve multidisciplinary plant design and management problems, taking into account both technical and non-technical constraints.

Students will develop the ability to work collaboratively and effectively within a team, understanding the context of plant engineering problems and recognizing their main interdisciplinary implications.
Students will be able to communicate information, problems and solutions in the field of industrial plants to both specialist and non-specialist audiences, using appropriate technical language.
Students will be able to graphically represent and communicate technical data, results and solutions through diagrams, graphs and tables.
Students will be able to identify and consult bibliographic sources and technical documentation (manuals, databases, digital resources), selecting relevant information.

Students will be able to understand and interpret the fundamental principles of design, production and maintenance processes, operating in compliance with quality, safety and reliability requirements and with reference to the main technical standards.

assessment_rules: The assessment is based on a written assignment consisting of 10 questions covering the entire program. Questions are of three types: simple theoretical (weight 1), average difficulty theoretical (weight 2), and articulated exercises (weight 3). To pass with a minimum score (18-22), students need a good overall knowledge and ability to model industrial engineering problems. High marks (26-28) require solid theoretical understanding, problem-solving, and critical analysis. The highest grade with honors (29-30 cum laude) is awarded for outstanding, comprehensive knowledge, independent operation in complex contexts, and excellent time management.
